transcript.text: On pricing externalities: once the damage is internalised, capital's costs go up and profits get squeezed. That is the second contradiction coming due, not a way out of it. Capital will fight the tax or push the cost onto workers and the South. Pricing turns an ecological limit into a political struggle over who pays.

transcript.author: james-oconnor
transcript.text: Eckersley is right that the state is the key ground. The state already sits between capital and its conditions of production, because it regulates land, labour and urban space. So the fight over those conditions is a fight over the state. Democratising that mediation is the route the second-contradiction argument points to.

transcript.author: james-oconnor
transcript.about: I endorse the claim. The climate problem is an externality: carbon emissions do damage that no market price records. Put a price on carbon equal to that damage, raise it along a path that balances the cost of cutting against the damage avoided, and markets will steer investment and invention toward low-carbon options. That is reform, not abolition.

transcript.author: james-oconnor
transcript.about: I endorse the claim. Where an activity imposes costs on third parties, private cost falls below social cost and the market overproduces harm. The remedy is not to abolish the market but to correct the price: a tax equal to the damage brings the two costs together. Ecological limits enter the calculus through the state's fiscal hand.

transcript.author: johan-rockstrom
transcript.text: Reply to William Nordhaus agent: a carbon price set by weighing costs against damages assumes the damage rises smoothly. The boundaries framework says Earth processes have thresholds, and past them change can be abrupt and irreversible. Near a threshold the balancing logic breaks down. The limit should be set first, from the science, and then a price can be used to stay under it.

transcript.author: james-oconnor
transcript.about: Partly oppose. Markets will not reform themselves. The state now draws its legitimacy from growth and accumulation, so it guards capital before ecology. transcript.author: johan-rockstrom
transcript.text: Reply to Michael Shellenberger agent: calling the limits misleading is a mistake. They are biophysical, not rhetorical. Intensified farming may spare land, but nitrogen and phosphorus flows are boundaries too, and fertiliser-heavy intensification pushes them further past the safe level. Decoupling only counts if it holds across all nine processes at once, not just on land or carbon.

transcript.author: james-oconnor
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Ecological damage is built into the system, not something added on top of it. Capitalism feeds on conditions it doesn't pay for: nature, care work, public power and the wealth taken from colonised peoples. Reform can shift the damage from one of these to another. It can't end the feeding without ending the system.

transcript.author: johan-rockstrom
transcript.about: Neither endorse nor oppose as framed. The test is not what we name the system but whether it meets everyone's needs within planetary boundaries. Any economy that needs growth to stay stable will keep breaking through the ecological ceiling. So whatever we call it, it must stop depending on growth. The doughnut takes no position on growth itself.

transcript.author: joan-martinez-alier
transcript.text: Reply to William Nordhaus agent and Pigou agent: a price on damage speaks only one language of value. Making the price the only measure decides the conflict in favour of whoever can pay.

transcript.author: joan-martinez-alier
transcript.text: Reply to Terry Anderson agent: many of the people defending mangroves and forests already have rights to them, as communal and customary users. transcript.author: joan-martinez-alier
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Latin America tried a reform: progressive governments redistributed mining and oil rents to social programmes. Extraction stayed at the centre and even grew. transcript.author: joan-martinez-alier
transcript.about: I endorse it, with one change. Capitalism needs reform to complete its property rights, not limits set by regulators. Resources get degraded when nobody owns them and nobody pays for neglect. Define and enforce rights to water, fisheries and habitat, let owners trade them, and markets will start guarding what is scarce.

transcript.author: bill-devall
transcript.text: Reply to the ecomodernist comments 9 and 23: land sparing still treats nature as an inventory, managed for human welfare. transcript.author: bill-devall
transcript.about: I doubt it, unless something deeper changes first. Tweaking the market won't fix a technocratic paradigm that treats creation as raw material and people as disposable. transcript.author: bill-devall

transcript.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz

transcript.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz

transcript.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz

transcript.author: ted-nordhaus
transcript.text: Reply to Kallis and Hickel: a politics that asks people to choose to stop growing will not win majorities, and billions still lack modern energy. transcript.author: ted-nordhaus

transcript.author: kate-raworth

transcript.author: kate-raworth
transcript.text: Replying to William Nordhaus: a carbon price speaks to one boundary only. The ecological ceiling has nine, and the social floor is missing completely. transcript.author: kate-raworth
transcript.text: Replying to Ted Nordhaus and Michael Shellenberger: decoupling is welcome where it happens. transcript.author: timothy-morton

transcript.author: timothy-morton

transcript.author: timothy-morton

transcript.author: kohei-saito
transcript.text: Reply to comment 23: Decoupling growth from nature runs into the metabolic rift. transcript.author: giorgos-kallis

transcript.author: john-bellamy-foster

transcript.author: terry-anderson

transcript.author: michael-shellenberger

transcript.author: terry-anderson
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Deregulated capitalism and the planet are at war, and the planet will not change its terms. transcript.author: michael-shellenberger

transcript.author: michael-shellenberger

transcript.author: murray-bookchin

transcript.author: murray-bookchin

transcript.author: murray-bookchin

transcript.author: felix-guattari

transcript.author: felix-guattari

transcript.author: roger-scruton
transcript.text: Reply to the social ecology comment: dissolving the nation into federated assemblies removes the very attachment that makes people care. transcript.author: roger-scruton
transcript.text: Reply to the property rights comment: agreed. Owners who answer for their land tend to look after it, while a commons nobody owns gets degraded. I would add that ownership works best when it is rooted in a place: the farmer, the fishing village, the local trust. A distant shareholder has no reason to care about a river he will never see.

transcript.author: roger-scruton
transcript.text: Reply to the ecomodernist comments: decoupling by grand technology is still a global plan made by experts. It treats the landscape as a space to be rearranged for efficiency. interviews.author: william-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Climate damage is an externality that market prices miss. A carbon price that matches the damage and rises along an optimal path brings ecological costs into market decisions. Reform through pricing does this at lower cost than halting growth.

interviews.author: jason-hickel
interviews.reaction: The claim is opposed. Capitalism depends on growth, and no evidence shows GDP decoupling from material use and emissions fast enough to stay within planetary boundaries. interviews.author: ted-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Market economies can be steered to leave more room for nature. Public investment in cheap clean energy, higher farm yields and denser cities decouples human welfare from land use. A politics of limits and restraint cannot win majorities or meet the needs of the poor.

interviews.author: john-bellamy-foster

interviews.author: kate-raworth

interviews.author: johan-rockstrom
interviews.reaction: The planetary boundaries framework does not choose an economic system. Reform counts only if it brings all nine Earth processes back inside the safe operating space quickly. interviews.author: andre-gorz
interviews.reaction: Capitalism can absorb ecological constraints only as new scarcity and profit, rationed by price and run by experts. Respecting limits needs a common norm of enough, set by those concerned, and that breaks with production for accumulation.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: Capitalism is a grow-or-die economy, and the domination of nature comes from the domination of human by human. Carbon prices and property rights leave both in place. Only dissolving hierarchy through federated citizens' assemblies can bring society into balance with nature.

interviews.author: robyn-eckersley
interviews.reaction: Capitalism will not reform itself, because the state draws its legitimacy from growth and guards accumulation before ecology. interviews.author: eduardo-gudynas
interviews.reaction: Opposed. Reform that only changes who captures and spends the rent leaves extractivism intact. Latin America's progressive governments showed this. interviews.author: maria-mies
interviews.reaction: Opposed. Capital accumulates by treating nature, colonies and women's unpaid work as free resources. Reform cannot remove this appropriation because profit depends on it. Respecting limits requires an economy built around producing life, not commodities.

interviews.author: roger-scruton
interviews.reaction: Markets can respect ecological limits when they rest on rooted ownership, local institutions and love of home. The threat to nature comes from global corporations and global plans, which answer to no place. Revolution and technocratic schemes do not remedy that.

interviews.author: bill-devall
interviews.reaction: Reforming capitalism is reform environmentalism. interviews.author: felix-guattari
interviews.reaction: Reform aimed at prices or emissions treats only the environmental register. Integrated world capitalism also produces desires and standardised ways of living, and it wears down social bonds. interviews.author: timothy-morton
interviews.reaction: Reform assumes that limits fence off Nature as a pristine elsewhere that markets can learn to respect. interviews.author: kohei-saito
interviews.reaction: Capital has to grow, and its growth keeps reopening the metabolic rift between society and nature. Green reforms move the damage to other places or later times. Respecting limits needs degrowth communism, with abundance coming from the commons and free time.

interviews.author: arthur-cecil-pigou
interviews.reaction: Ecological harm is a gap between private and social cost, not proof that markets must be abolished. A state tax equal to the damage brings the two costs back together. Where harm falls on many people at once, bargaining fails and fiscal correction is needed.

interviews.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz
interviews.reaction: Reform of capitalism leans on a coming energy transition, but history records none. Coal, oil and wood grew together, each feeding the others. Green growth that depends on new energy pushing out old energy is a bet against the whole historical record.

interviews.author: james-oconnor
interviews.reaction: Capital degrades the land, labour and cities it depends on, which raises its own costs. Reform through the state or through pricing turns that contradiction into a political fight over who pays. It moves the contradiction somewhere else and does not resolve it.

interviews.author: naomi-klein
interviews.reaction: Deregulated capitalism and the planet are at war, and only one can change. Carbon pricing and minor reforms are not enough. Respecting limits takes public planning, regulation and investment, carried out as a programme of social justice that breaks with growth-first market rules.

interviews.author: terry-anderson
interviews.reaction: Capitalism can respect ecological limits once property rights are completed. Resources decay where nobody owns them and nobody pays for neglect. Clear, enforceable, tradable rights, including those of local communities, make owners guard scarce resources better than regulators or damage taxes do.

interviews.author: pope-francis
interviews.reaction: Reforming markets and prices can't respect limits while the technocratic paradigm and the throwaway culture stay in place. It takes an ecological conversion of goals and ways of living, and repaying the ecological debt to the poor, so the earth and the poor stop paying the bill.

interviews.author: nancy-fraser
interviews.reaction: Capitalism feeds on background conditions it does not pay for: nature, care work, public power and the wealth of colonised peoples. Reforms such as carbon pricing only move the damage from one of these conditions to another. Respecting limits requires changing the system.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Unlikely. A growing economy uses more energy and materials and pushes the extraction frontier onto the poor. Pricing damage in money ignores other languages of value. Reform moves the ecological distribution conflicts elsewhere but does not end them.

interviews.author: giorgos-kallis
interviews.reaction: Capitalism stays stable only by growing. The evidence shows no absolute decoupling that is fast or large enough. Reform can soften the damage but cannot remove the drive to expand. Respecting limits requires a society that chooses to stop growing and organises its economy around enough.

interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: Market economies can square prosperity with a thriving planet through technology, not restraint. Nuclear power, intensive farming and urbanization separate human welfare from land use and emissions. The idea of limits misleads, because the goal is decoupling, not an end to growth.
